Key objective findings: isolated left eyelid ptosis (MRD1 1 mm vs 3 mm on right), impaired left blink reflex, left orbicularis oris weakness, left periorbital myokymia, and reproducible eyelid closure with mouth movement (synkinesis). Extraocular movements intact in all directions and pupils/light reflexes normal. MRI brain/MRA reported no obvious inflammatory lesions in the cranial nerve regions. Onset began 3 days after a vaccine dose and progressed over days; minimal subsequent improvement. No vesicular rash, hearing/taste intact, forehead wrinkling preserved.

Anatomic and pathophysiologic synthesis:
- The combination of impaired blink reflex and orbicularis (ocular) weakness points to dysfunction of the facial nerve motor limb (CN VII) on the left (peripheral facial nerve involvement). Blink reflex abnormality supports a peripheral motor defect rather than isolated neuromuscular junction disease.
- Preserved forehead wrinkling is an unusual finding for a classic complete peripheral (LMN) facial palsy because the frontalis is often involved; this pattern could reflect a selective/partial branch lesion of the facial nerve (distal branch involvement) or patchy involvement of the nerve. The presence of orbicularis oris weakness argues against a purely distal temporal-branch lesion and supports more proximal involvement of CN VII motor fibers, though the distribution is somewhat mixed.
- Synkinesis (eyelid closure with mouth movement) and myokymic activity suggest aberrant facial nerve excitation/irritation or prior regeneration-related miswiring. However, true aberrant regeneration/synkinesis typically appears weeks–months after nerve injury, so an acute-onset synkinetic pattern is atypical and raises two possibilities: an irritative/irregular firing phenomenon of the nerve (e.g., hyperexcitability/irritation) or misinterpretation of forced co-contraction on exam. Hemifacial spasm (vascular compression) commonly causes myokymia and synkinesis but usually does not cause weakness.

- A central (cortical) supranuclear stroke classically spares the forehead and causes contralateral lower facial weakness, but it would not explain an impaired blink reflex (a peripheral motor limb abnormality) or the periorbital myokymia/synkinesis, and MRI was negative for obvious lesions.
